Thanda Choir

By: Jo Munnik | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A global success story or a sophisticated scam? We go behind the scenes of the world-famous Thanda Choir to find out why South Africa’s 'internet darlings' are performing for the world while starvi

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive Access: This is the first time the choir has broken their collective silence. Carte Blanche has the sole opportunity to document the "unmasking" of a global sensation, providing a narrative that contrasts their public "love" persona with a private reality of systemic exploitation.
High-Impact Media Synergy: The story offers a prime opportunity for multi-platform collaboration. Given the choir's digital-first fame, the investigation is primed for viral reach across social media, radio, and international print, ensuring it remains a headline-dominating topic across all demographics.
Unprecedented Public Interest: With a collective reach of millions of followers, the Thanda Choir is one of South Africa’s most visible cultural exports of the decade. Any disruption to their narrative is guaranteed to spark massive local and international engagement, tapping into a global audience that feels personally invested in their success.
International Celebrity Involvement: The narrative extends beyond South African borders, featuring high-profile international elements. This includes the potential for exclusive commentary and interview requests from global icons like The Dave Matthews Band, Melody Gardot, and Memphis Depay, all of whom have been unwittingly drawn into the choir’s orbit.
A Landmark Social Justice Case: At its core, this is a story of Transformation vs. Exploitation. It tackles the intersection of race, class, and the "gig economy," highlighting the vulnerability of township artists against affluent, private-school-educated management. It is a powerful pursuit of justice for a "national treasure" being held hostage by its own success.


Summary:
The Thanda Choir is South Africa’s latest global export, a soaring beacon of hope rising from the under-resourced streets of Khayelitsha to the shortlists of the Oscars. With a social media following in the millions, they have transitioned from a local community group into a star-studded sensation, sharing stages with the Dave Matthews Band and Melody Gardot, while performing for elite global entities like META, Prudential, and international football star Memphis Depay.
To the world, they are the "darlings of the internet" and a vivid symbol of South African transformation—but as the choir’s global profile skyrockets, a discordant pattern of professional and financial abuse is emerging behind the scenes.
While the choir's management markets a story of empowerment, the singers themselves are trapped in a cycle of poverty that stands in chilling contrast to their fame. On average, these world-class performers earn a staggering pittance of just R400 a month, supplemented by a food hamper valued at R250. When members dare to question this meagre stipend, management reportedly weaponises the choir’s namesake, "Thanda," telling the singers they should perform for "love" rather than money. Those who persist in seeking transparency are met with retaliatory expulsion.
The numbers simply do not add up. While the performers struggle to survive, nearly R400,000 in donations intended for the choir’s upliftment remains unaccounted for, alongside at least R600,000 in performance fees generated since November alone—and that is a conservative estimate based only the figures that have come to light.
The choir now fears their funds are being siphoned by their management: two 21-year-old, private-school-educated men from affluent backgrounds who allegedly funnel payments into private accounts to "avoid tax." Despite being registered as an NPO, there are claims that no income is being declared to SARS, leaving the choir’s legal and financial standing in jeopardy.
Now, trapped between their lifelong passion for music and the crushing weight of exploitation, the members of Thanda Choir are finally breaking their silence, in an exclusive. They are a "family" terrified of losing their purpose, yet they can no longer ignore the R400 barrier that stands between their global success and their personal dignity.


Further information:
INVESTIGATION ELEMENTS


The "Passion" Trap & Coercive Tactics:
When members question their R400 monthly stipend, management allegedly weaponises the choir’s namesake, telling singers they should perform for "love," not money.
Those who persist are met with retaliatory expulsion and character assassination.
Several choir members have been expelled following financial inquiries and the mother of a member claims to have received an offer for a bribe to silence her questions around finances.
The Shadow Economy:
While the group is registered as an NPO, the "non-profit" status appears to be a front. (I’m in the process of verifying the NPO number but no luck so far.)
Performance fees and high-profile corporate payments are reportedly funneled directly into a ABSA personal bank account. When asked why, the manager told the group "to avoid tax."
For over two years, management has ignored all formal requests for bank statements, making internal audits impossible and leaving the choir’s true earnings a mystery.
The "Ghost" Donations: Philanthropy or Piracy?
The betrayal doesn't stop at the choir; it extends to the global stage. High-profile international icons, including the Dave Matthews Band, have lent their names and deep pockets to the cause, spearheading massive donation drives.
On the Thanda Choir’s own website, figures between $15,000 and $30,000 (approx. 4000,000) are proudly displayed as "successfully raised" for "building fees" and "studio equipment."
Yet, while these digital trackers remain live and the donation portals stay open, the choir’s reality is a world away from "upliftment." Despite the almost half-a-million Rand supposedly earmarked for their infrastructure, the singers continue to rehearse in borrowed, temporary spaces and know nothing about what has happened to the funds raised.
One of the big fundraising drives involved choir members cycling the Argus/ Cycle tour, they were promised compensation but received none and the bicycles that were donated were taken away and allegedly sold.
IP Theft & Commercial Piracy:
Despite composing original hits for major global brands and Oscar-nominated films, the creators report they have seen zero royalties. In fact, they did not even know they were entitled to them.
In one instance, the choir only became aware that one of their original songs had been used in the Orlando Pirates documentary when they saw it on TV.
The Oscar nominated Last Ranger producer has confirmed that the choir was paid both for the composition and to perform at a screening. Yet, the choir and composer knows nothing about this.
Management has allegedly sold these original compositions to corporations while denying the artists any authorship fees, effectively hijacking the choir’s intellectual property seemingly for private gain.

THE MONEY THAT WE KNOW OF


Total Unaccounted Funds: ~R1,000,000

To date, approximately $22,000 (±R400,000) has been raised via online platforms, including a high-profile campaign in conjunction with the Dave Matthews Band. While the stated purpose of these funds was to construct a rehearsal space and support community upliftment, no such facility exists. Furthermore, the choir members have not been informed of the location or allocation of these funds nor know where this facility is supposed to be..

Based on confirmed booking rates of R40,000 per 45-minute performance, an audit of gigs from November 2025 to March 2026 reveals a significant surplus. After deducting known operational expenses—including member stipends, food parcels, management fees, and transport—there remains an unaccounted balance of approximately R600,000.


The combined total of missing donor funds and performance revenue exceeds R1 million. As a registered NPO, all funds must be transparently accounted for.

ADDITIONAL INTERVIEWS OFF CAMERA

To verify actual amounts paid by local and international clients for performances, compositions and licensing.
To verify what donations were raised for according to the donors

BACKGROUND

Origin and Mission
Derived from the Xhosa word for "love," Thanda Choir was established in Khayelitsha, Cape Town, as a creative sanctuary and surrogate family for youth facing systemic poverty and crime. What began as a community haven has evolved into a high-output professional ensemble of 40 members, aged mid-teens to mid-twenties. The group’s creative "heartbeat" is led by conductor/composer Prince and lead vocalist Asandisa.
Management and Governance
The choir is managed by Luke and Julio, who discovered the group busking on YouTube three years ago. At age 19, they assumed total control over branding, commercial bookings, and digital assets.
Operational Gap: Management resides in Cape Town central and rarely attends rehearsals, employing "community managers" to oversee daily operations.
Administrative Discrepancies: While the choir is rooted in Khayelitsha, the official business address is listed at a private residence in Johannesburg. The legitimacy of their Non-Profit Organisation (NPO) status remains unverified.
Digital Footprint and Global Recognition
Thanda Choir has achieved "internet sensation" status through a meticulously managed digital strategy that contrasts sharply with the members' lived realities.
Social Reach: A combined following of over 1 million.
Viral Milestones: Their 2025 "Paris street performances" garnered over 8.4 million views on Instagram. The "Hata" rehearsal video (420k+ views) sparked a global "reaction video" trend.
Streaming & Media: With 41,000 monthly Spotify listeners, the group has been featured on The Expresso Show and opened for Melody Gardot at the legendary L’Olympia in Paris. High-profile endorsements include Viola Davis, the Dave Matthews Band, and footballer Memphis Depay.
Allegations of Exploitation
Despite significant commercial success and international tours, a deep-seated pattern of financial and professional exploitation is alleged:
The "Stipend" System: Senior members earn a monthly stipend of R400, contingent on 80% rehearsal attendance (approx. R10/hour). Pay is frequently substituted with basic food parcels.
Touring Discrepancies: For a three-week tour in France, members received a lump sum of R8,500; a week-long Brazil tour paid just R1,500. There are concerns regarding the interception of international per diems (€40/day).
IP Theft: Original compositions have reportedly been sold to major brands (Carling Black Label, Orlando Pirates) without royalties or credits reaching the creators.
Coercion and Lack of Transparency
Management allegedly maintains control through psychological and physical intimidation:
Retaliation: Members requesting transparency face character assassination, demotion, or expulsion.
Gatekeeping: Management maintains exclusive access to all social media revenue, ad-sense, and donation channels.
Misappropriation: Significant donations from international icons intended for a dedicated rehearsal space and equipment remain unaccounted for; the choir continues to rehearse in a free community hall.

Press Release:


Harmony or Hustle?
A global success story or a sophisticated scam? They’re internet darlings, drawing applause on the global stage. But even as they perform for the world, the stars of a celebrated choir are struggling to survive. At home: allegations of exploitation, intimidation, and stolen intellectual property. Management markets a story of empowerment, while singers are trapped in a cycle of poverty. They say they have no power over their time, their money – or their music. And now, for the first time, they’re breaking their silence.
Producer: Jo Munnik | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


CARTE BLANCHE II THANDA CHOIR SCRIPT
Producer : Jo Munnik

IN CAPE TOWN A MODERN DAVID AND GOLIATH STORY IS TAKING SHAPE.
ASANDISA SISWANA AND LISAKHANYA “PRINCE” MAQHAJANA COME FROM HUMBLE BACKGROUNDS, BROUGHT TOGETHER BY A SHARED PASSION FOR MUSIC. THEY STARTED THEIR CAREERS BUSKING FOR CHANGE ON THE STREETS OF CAPE TOWN; TODAY, THEY FIND THEMSELVES AS THE FACES OF SOUTH AFRICA’S NEWEST MUSICAL POWERHOUSE- THE THANDA CHOIR.
CLAIRE MAWISA PTC
On social media they are shown to be a global music sensation. But back home in Khayelitsha, Thanda Choir’s reality is very different.

Asandisa Siswana , Thanda Choir ( Xhosa With Subs): When people meet with you here, you get, "Phavi, yoo! I used to go to school with Asandisa. She's in Paris, etc. Now, when you get back here in the township and someone requests you to buy cooldrink... "No, I don't have (money)."
Claire Mawisa ( Xhosa With Subs): How? You were in Paris…
Asandisa Siswana , Thanda Choir ( Xhosa With Subs): It doesn’t make sense.

BEHIND THE SCENES, THE CHOIR MEMBERS STRUGGLE TO SURVIVE. THEY HOLD NO POWER OVER THEIR MUSIC, THEIR MONEY, OR THEIR TIME. MANAGEMENT HOLDS ALL THE STRINGS.

Lisakhanya “Prince” Maqhajana , Thanda Choir ( Xhosa With Subs): We rehearse from Monday to Friday. But most of the time, we do have gigs.So, it's always packed.
Claire Mawisa: This sounds like it's a full time job?
Asandisa Siswana , Thanda Choir: Ya, it is
Lisakhanya “Prince” Maqhajana , Thanda Choir: It is full-time.

THE GRIND IS RELENTLESS. MEMBERS FACE A BRUTAL CHOICE: THEIR WELLBEING OR THE MUSIC.

Zizipho Mathontsi, Thanda Choir :I am unemployed.I made sacrifices, I dropped out of school.
Because everything was so promising.

LEAD VOCALIST ZIZIPHO MATHONTSI ABANDONED HER TEACHING DEGREE TO MEET THE DEMANDING SCHEDULE.

THE PAYOFF? A PITTANCE.

Claire Mawisa: How much are you, or how much are choir members being paid?
Lisakhanya “Prince” Maqhajana , Thanda Choir (Xhosa and English mixed with subs): The members are paid 400 a month. And the R400, it's not for gigs. It's for participating in the rehearsals. If you attend 80% of your rehearsals a month, then you stand a chance of getting that 400. For local gigs we do not get any money.
Claire Mawisa: Yeh?!
Asandisa & Prince, Thanda Choir: Ya, at all!

FROM THE START, TWO 22-YEAR-OLDS HAVE HELD THE REINS: JULIO TEIXEIRA AND LUKE BERNHARDI. THEY REGISTERED THE CHOIR AS AN NPO WITH THEMSELVES AS DIRECTORS—CONTROLLING EVERY CENT, EVERY POST, AND EVERY BOOKING. WE CALL TO ASK WHAT THEY CHARGE.

Luke Bernhardi, Thanda Choir: At the moment, for kind of private stuff, we're charging about R40 000 for a 45-minute to an hour set.

SCENE: GFX TO ILLUSTRATE THE NUMBERS

OUR INVESTIGATION REVEALS THE CHOIR AVERAGES SIX GIGS A MONTH. IN THE WEEK OF FILMING, THEY BOOK SIX GIGS IN JUST SEVEN DAYS. AT R40,000 A SET, THAT’S A QUARTER OF A MILLION RAND. YET, TWENTY-FIVE SENIOR MEMBERS EARN JUST R400 A MONTH, WHILE ALL 40 MEMBERS RECEIVE A R250 FOOD HAMPER. THE MATHS DOESN'T ADD UP.

Claire Mawisa: You don’t know how much Thanda Choir charges per gig? Must I tell you?
Zizipho Mathontsi, Thanda Choir: Ya, you can.
Claire Mawisa: Per event, Luke and Julio charge 40 000 rand for 45-minute performance for Thanda Choir.
Claire Mawisa: So after six gigs its a quarter of a million rand.
Zizipho Mathontsi, Thanda Choir: [sighs ]I don’t know what to say. [cries]
Zizipho Mathontsi, Thanda Choir: Actually, we don't know anything. We just go to rehearsal; we do performances only.
Claire Mawisa: For a 400 rand sisi?
Zizipho Mathontsi, Thanda Choir: And food parcel…

VO
WE ASK ENTERTAINMENT LAWYER DAVID FEINBERG TO WEIGH IN.

Claire Mawisa: Is it an obligation on the management side to be completely transparent with the money that is being earned by the artist?
David Feinberg, Entertainment Lawyer: Absolutely. The reason for that is that the manager is placed in a position of authority and power. If they are receiving money, then they have an obligation to ensure that they can account for that and that there is a mechanism for transparency.

SLIDE SHOWING ALLEGATIONS - GFX

BUT A LACK OF TRANSPARENCY IS ONLY THE BEGINNING. LUKE AND JULIO FACE A LITANY OF ALLEGATIONS: UNACCOUNTED INCOME, WITHHELD WAGES, UNRECONCILED DONATIONS, STOLEN COPYRIGHT, AND INTIMIDATION.


IT’S TIME FOR ANSWERS. WE REQUEST AN INTERVIEW AT THE CHOIR’S DILAPIDATED REHEARSAL SHACK.

Claire Mawisa: How much do choir members earn?
Julio Teixeira, Thanda Choir: I don't want to put the information out there publicly.
Claire Mawisa: We’ve been told that stipend is R 400 a month.
Julio Teixeira, Thanda Choir: Yes. That is, that is true it is R 400 a month.
Claire Mawisa: How much do you charge per local gig for the choir?
Julio Teixeira, Thanda Choir: We can tell you that off record.
Claire Mawisa: I know how much you charge per gig - 40,000 rand for 45 minutes.
Julio Teixeira, Thanda Choir: Yes.
Luke Bernhardi, Thanda Choir: I manage the bookings and it depends on what the inquiry is.
Claire Mawisa: We literally have a recording of you because we'll try to book the gig.
Luke Bernhardi, Thanda Choir: Yes.
Claire Mawisa: So if the choir is going on to perform, for example, tonight, do they get a cut of that 40,000 rand for local gigs?
Luke Bernhardi, Thanda Choir: No, because that's what we used to fund the organisation.
Claire Mawisa: If in a week or in a month, you've got five, six, eight gigs. So that's around 200,000 rand you're talking about. So what are we spending the money on?
Julio Teixeira, Thanda Choir: …. like legal and accounting fees but then also like uniform Tommy takkies., we will decide what is most pressing.

Summary: The Thanda Choir is South Africa’s latest global export, a soaring beacon of hope rising from the under-resourced streets of Khayelitsha to the shortlists of the Oscars. With a social media following in the millions, they have transitioned from a local community group into a star-studded sensation, sharing stages with the Dave Matthews Band and Melody Gardot, while performing for elite global entities like META, Prudential, and international football star Memphis Depay. To the world, they are the "darlings of the internet" and a vivid symbol of South African transformation—but as the choir’s global profile skyrockets, a discordant pattern of professional and financial abuse is emerging behind the scenes. While the choir's management markets a story of empowerment, the singers themselves are trapped in a cycle of poverty that stands in chilling contrast to their fame. On average, these world-class performers earn a staggering pittance of just R400 a month, supplemented by a food hamper valued at R250. When members dare to question this meagre stipend, management reportedly weaponises the choir’s namesake, "Thanda," telling the singers they should perform for "love" rather than money. Those who persist in seeking transparency are met with retaliatory expulsion. The numbers simply do not add up. While the performers struggle to survive, nearly R400,000 in donations intended for the choir’s upliftment remains unaccounted for, alongside at least R600,000 in performance fees generated since November alone—and that is a conservative estimate based only the figures that have come to light. The choir now fears their funds are being siphoned by their management: two 21-year-old, private-school-educated men from affluent backgrounds who allegedly funnel payments into private accounts to "avoid tax." Despite being registered as an NPO, there are claims that no income is being declared to SARS, leaving the choir’s legal and financial standing in jeopardy. Now, trapped between their lifelong passion for music and the crushing weight of exploitation, the members of Thanda Choir are finally breaking their silence, in an exclusive. They are a "family" terrified of losing their purpose, yet they can no longer ignore the R400 barrier that stands between their global success and their personal dignity. Further information: INVESTIGATION ELEMENTS The "Passion" Trap & Coercive Tactics: When members question their R400 monthly stipend, management allegedly weaponises the choir’s namesake, telling singers they should perform for "love," not money. Those who persist are met with retaliatory expulsion and character assassination. Several choir members have been expelled following financial inquiries and the mother of a member claims to have received an offer for a bribe to silence her questions around finances. The Shadow Economy: While the group is registered as an NPO, the "non-profit" status appears to be a front. (I’m in the process of verifying the NPO number but no luck so far.) Performance fees and high-profile corporate payments are reportedly funneled directly into a ABSA personal bank account. When asked why, the manager told the group "to avoid tax." For over two years, management has ignored all formal requests for bank statements, making internal audits impossible and leaving the choir’s true earnings a mystery. The "Ghost" Donations: Philanthropy or Piracy? The betrayal doesn't stop at the choir; it extends to the global stage. High-profile international icons, including the Dave Matthews Band, have lent their names and deep pockets to the cause, spearheading massive donation drives. On the Thanda Choir’s own website, figures between $15,000 and $30,000 (approx. 4000,000) are proudly displayed as "successfully raised" for "building fees" and "studio equipment." Yet, while these digital trackers remain live and the donation portals stay open, the choir’s reality is a world away from "upliftment." Despite the almost half-a-million Rand supposedly earmarked for their infrastructure, the singers continue to rehearse in borrowed, temporary spaces and know nothing about what has happened to the funds raised. One of the big fundraising drives involved choir members cycling the Argus/ Cycle tour, they were promised compensation but received none and the bicycles that were donated were taken away and allegedly sold. IP Theft & Commercial Piracy: Despite composing original hits for major global brands and Oscar-nominated films, the creators report they have seen zero royalties. In fact, they did not even know they were entitled to them. In one instance, the choir only became aware that one of their original songs had been used in the Orlando Pirates documentary when they saw it on TV. The Oscar nominated Last Ranger producer has confirmed that the choir was paid both for the composition and to perform at a screening. Yet, the choir and composer knows nothing about this. Management has allegedly sold these original compositions to corporations while denying the artists any authorship fees, effectively hijacking the choir’s intellectual property seemingly for private gain. THE MONEY THAT WE KNOW OF Total Unaccounted Funds: ~R1,000,000 To date, approximately $22,000 (±R400,000) has been raised via online platforms, including a high-profile campaign in conjunction with the Dave Matthews Band. While the stated purpose of these funds was to construct a rehearsal space and support community upliftment, no such facility exists. Furthermore, the choir members have not been informed of the location or allocation of these funds nor know where this facility is supposed to be.. Based on confirmed booking rates of R40,000 per 45-minute performance, an audit of gigs from November 2025 to March 2026 reveals a significant surplus. After deducting known operational expenses—including member stipends, food parcels, management fees, and transport—there remains an unaccounted balance of approximately R600,000. The combined total of missing donor funds and performance revenue exceeds R1 million. As a registered NPO, all funds must be transparently accounted for. What began as a community haven has evolved into a high-output professional ensemble of 40 members, aged mid-teens to mid-twenties. The group’s creative "heartbeat" is led by conductor/composer Prince and lead vocalist Asandisa. Management and Governance The choir is managed by Luke and Julio, who discovered the group busking on YouTube three years ago. At age 19, they assumed total control over branding, commercial bookings, and digital assets. Operational Gap: Management resides in Cape Town central and rarely attends rehearsals, employing "community managers" to oversee daily operations. Administrative Discrepancies: While the choir is rooted in Khayelitsha, the official business address is listed at a private residence in Johannesburg. The legitimacy of their Non-Profit Organisation (NPO) status remains unverified. Gatekeeping: Management maintains exclusive access to all social media revenue, ad-sense, and donation channels. Misappropriation: Significant donations from international icons intended for a dedicated rehearsal space and equipment remain unaccounted for; the choir continues to rehearse in a free community hall. metadata.Summary: The Thanda Choir is South Africa’s latest global export, a soaring beacon of hope rising from the under-resourced streets of Khayelitsha to the shortlists of the Oscars. With a social media following in the millions, they have transitioned from a local community group into a star-studded sensation, sharing stages with the Dave Matthews Band and Melody Gardot, while performing for elite global entities like META, Prudential, and international football star Memphis Depay. To the world, they are the "darlings of the internet" and a vivid symbol of South African transformation—but as the choir’s global profile skyrockets, a discordant pattern of professional and financial abuse is emerging behind the scenes. While the choir's management markets a story of empowerment, the singers themselves are trapped in a cycle of poverty that stands in chilling contrast to their fame. On average, these world-class performers earn a staggering pittance of just R400 a month, supplemented by a food hamper valued at R250. When members dare to question this meagre stipend, management reportedly weaponises the choir’s namesake, "Thanda," telling the singers they should perform for "love" rather than money. Those who persist in seeking transparency are met with retaliatory expulsion. The numbers simply do not add up. While the performers struggle to survive, nearly R400,000 in donations intended for the choir’s upliftment remains unaccounted for, alongside at least R600,000 in performance fees generated since November alone—and that is a conservative estimate based only the figures that have come to light. The choir now fears their funds are being siphoned by their management: two 21-year-old, private-school-educated men from affluent backgrounds who allegedly funnel payments into private accounts to "avoid tax." Despite being registered as an NPO, there are claims that no income is being declared to SARS, leaving the choir’s legal and financial standing in jeopardy. Now, trapped between their lifelong passion for music and the crushing weight of exploitation, the members of Thanda Choir are finally breaking their silence, in an exclusive. They are a "family" terrified of losing their purpose, yet they can no longer ignore the R400 barrier that stands between their global success and their personal dignity.
metadata.Further information: INVESTIGATION ELEMENTS The "Passion" Trap & Coercive Tactics: When members question their R400 monthly stipend, management allegedly weaponises the choir’s namesake, telling singers they should perform for "love," not money. Those who persist are met with retaliatory expulsion and character assassination. Several choir members have been expelled following financial inquiries and the mother of a member claims to have received an offer for a bribe to silence her questions around finances. The Shadow Economy: While the group is registered as an NPO, the "non-profit" status appears to be a front. (I’m in the process of verifying the NPO number but no luck so far.) Performance fees and high-profile corporate payments are reportedly funneled directly into a ABSA personal bank account. When asked why, the manager told the group "to avoid tax." For over two years, management has ignored all formal requests for bank statements, making internal audits impossible and leaving the choir’s true earnings a mystery. The "Ghost" Donations: Philanthropy or Piracy? The betrayal doesn't stop at the choir; it extends to the global stage. High-profile international icons, including the Dave Matthews Band, have lent their names and deep pockets to the cause, spearheading massive donation drives. On the Thanda Choir’s own website, figures between $15,000 and $30,000 (approx. 4000,000) are proudly displayed as "successfully raised" for "building fees" and "studio equipment." Yet, while these digital trackers remain live and the donation portals stay open, the choir’s reality is a world away from "upliftment." Despite the almost half-a-million Rand supposedly earmarked for their infrastructure, the singers continue to rehearse in borrowed, temporary spaces and know nothing about what has happened to the funds raised. One of the big fundraising drives involved choir members cycling the Argus/ Cycle tour, they were promised compensation but received none and the bicycles that were donated were taken away and allegedly sold. IP Theft & Commercial Piracy: Despite composing original hits for major global brands and Oscar-nominated films, the creators report they have seen zero royalties. In fact, they did not even know they were entitled to them. In one instance, the choir only became aware that one of their original songs had been used in the Orlando Pirates documentary when they saw it on TV. The Oscar nominated Last Ranger producer has confirmed that the choir was paid both for the composition and to perform at a screening. Yet, the choir and composer knows nothing about this. Management has allegedly sold these original compositions to corporations while denying the artists any authorship fees, effectively hijacking the choir’s intellectual property seemingly for private gain. THE MONEY THAT WE KNOW OF Total Unaccounted Funds: ~R1,000,000 To date, approximately $22,000 (±R400,000) has been raised via online platforms, including a high-profile campaign in conjunction with the Dave Matthews Band. While the stated purpose of these funds was to construct a rehearsal space and support community upliftment, no such facility exists. Furthermore, the choir members have not been informed of the location or allocation of these funds nor know where this facility is supposed to be.. Based on confirmed booking rates of R40,000 per 45-minute performance, an audit of gigs from November 2025 to March 2026 reveals a significant surplus. After deducting known operational expenses—including member stipends, food parcels, management fees, and transport—there remains an unaccounted balance of approximately R600,000. The combined total of missing donor funds and performance revenue exceeds R1 million. As a registered NPO, all funds must be transparently accounted for. ADDITIONAL INTERVIEWS OFF CAMERA To verify actual amounts paid by local and international clients for performances, compositions and licensing. To verify what donations were raised for according to the donors BACKGROUND Origin and Mission Derived from the Xhosa word for "love," Thanda Choir was established in Khayelitsha, Cape Town, as a creative sanctuary and surrogate family for youth facing systemic poverty and crime. What began as a community haven has evolved into a high-output professional ensemble of 40 members, aged mid-teens to mid-twenties. The group’s creative "heartbeat" is led by conductor/composer Prince and lead vocalist Asandisa. Management and Governance The choir is managed by Luke and Julio, who discovered the group busking on YouTube three years ago. At age 19, they assumed total control over branding, commercial bookings, and digital assets. Operational Gap: Management resides in Cape Town central and rarely attends rehearsals, employing "community managers" to oversee daily operations. Administrative Discrepancies: While the choir is rooted in Khayelitsha, the official business address is listed at a private residence in Johannesburg. The legitimacy of their Non-Profit Organisation (NPO) status remains unverified. Digital Footprint and Global Recognition Thanda Choir has achieved "internet sensation" status through a meticulously managed digital strategy that contrasts sharply with the members' lived realities. Social Reach: A combined following of over 1 million. Viral Milestones: Their 2025 "Paris street performances" garnered over 8.4 million views on Instagram. The "Hata" rehearsal video (420k+ views) sparked a global "reaction video" trend. Streaming & Media: With 41,000 monthly Spotify listeners, the group has been featured on The Expresso Show and opened for Melody Gardot at the legendary L’Olympia in Paris. High-profile endorsements include Viola Davis, the Dave Matthews Band, and footballer Memphis Depay. Allegations of Exploitation Despite significant commercial success and international tours, a deep-seated pattern of financial and professional exploitation is alleged: The "Stipend" System: Senior members earn a monthly stipend of R400, contingent on 80% rehearsal attendance (approx. R10/hour). Pay is frequently substituted with basic food parcels. Touring Discrepancies: For a three-week tour in France, members received a lump sum of R8,500; a week-long Brazil tour paid just R1,500. There are concerns regarding the interception of international per diems (€40/day). IP Theft: Original compositions have reportedly been sold to major brands (Carling Black Label, Orlando Pirates) without royalties or credits reaching the creators. Coercion and Lack of Transparency Management allegedly maintains control through psychological and physical intimidation: Retaliation: Members requesting transparency face character assassination, demotion, or expulsion. Gatekeeping: Management maintains exclusive access to all social media revenue, ad-sense, and donation channels. Misappropriation: Significant donations from international icons intended for a dedicated rehearsal space and equipment remain unaccounted for; the choir continues to rehearse in a free community hall.
